Empirical Research Plan – “Do Female Village Leaders Allocate Public Resources Differently?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen strategy: Two-stage least squares (instrumental variables).

Why IV is appropriate
•	The gender of the Pradhan (chief) may be endogenous: unusually progressive villages might voluntarily elect women, and such villages may already invest differently.  
•	The 73rd Amendment’s legally mandated, rotating reservation of every third seat for a woman provides an externally assigned shock to the probability that a GP is headed by a woman.  
•	The reservation rule is as‐good‐as‐random within a district because serial legislative numbers were set decades earlier and are unrelated to current needs or preferences.  
•	Thus “seat reserved for women” is a strong, plausibly exogenous instrument for “Pradhan is female,” delivering the local average treatment effect (LATE) of female leadership on public-goods allocations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor)  
 FemalePradhanᵍ = 1 if the GP’s elected Pradhan in 1998/2000 is a woman, 0 otherwise.

Instrument (assignment)  
 ReservedSeatᵍ = 1 if the GP seat was legally reserved for a woman in the 1998 election, 0 otherwise.

Control group / counterfactual  
 GPs that were not reserved and therefore (in most cases) elected male Pradhans.

Timing  
 Treatment starts with the May 1998 election in West Bengal and the 1995 election in Rajasthan; outcomes are measured over the subsequent ≈ 2 years (1998-2000 WB, 1995-1997 RAJ).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Relevance – Reservation strongly increases the probability of a female Pradhan.  
 Plausible: in most Indian states compliance is > 90 percent; we will report the first-stage F-statistic.

A2. Exclusion – Reservation affects public‐goods outcomes only through the gender of the Pradhan, not via other channels.  
 Plausible but requires discussion. Funds, statutory powers, and voter demographics are unchanged; the only mandated difference is that the seat must be filled by a woman. We test by controlling for Pradhan education, age, caste, and prior experience.

A3. Independence (as-good-as-random assignment) – Conditional on district fixed effects, ReservedSeat is orthogonal to pre-treatment village characteristics.  
 Plausible because the serial numbers were set historically for administrative convenience. We will confirm balance on 1991 Census characteristics and pre-1998 infrastructure.

A4. Monotonicity – A GP that is female when unreserved will also be female when reserved (no “defiers”).  
 Highly plausible; reservation can only push GPs toward, not away from, electing women.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no cross-GP spillovers) – One GP’s reservation status does not affect another GP’s investments.  
 Reasonable because funds are allocated at the GP level and budgets are not pooled.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Imperfect compliance / proxy leadership (husbands of female Pradhans make decisions).  
Mitigation: (i) Use the administrative gender on the ballot (what voters observe) since that is what reservation directly changes; (ii) collect proxy variables such as “husband attends meetings” and show that results are robust to excluding those cases.

Threat 2: Serial-number ordering might correlate with unobserved geography (e.g., the first GP in a block could be closer to roads).  
Mitigation: Include block or sub-district fixed effects and pre-treatment geographic controls; run placebo regressions of ReservedSeat on 1991 outcomes to verify no systematic differences.

Threat 3: Heterogeneous funding cycles could confound the 2-year investment window.  
Mitigation: Use outcomes expressed as shares of total GP expenditure; add control for total GP budget; run robustness restricting to infrastructure that can be completed quickly (hand pumps, small roads).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional IV
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
gp  <- read_csv("gp_level_westbengal.csv")        # 161 obs
raj <- read_csv("gp_level_rajasthan.csv")         # 100 obs
data <- bind_rows(gp, raj) %>% 
         mutate(district = factor(district))

# 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------------
data <- data %>% 
  mutate(
    FemalePradhan   = if_else(pradhan_gender == "F", 1, 0),
    ReservedSeat    = if_else(seat_reserved_women == 1, 1, 0),
    # Example outcome: share of new expenditures on drinking water
    WaterShare      = new_spend_water / total_new_spend,
    RoadShare       = new_spend_roads  / total_new_spend
  )

# 3. Baseline balance check ----------------------------------------
balance_vars <- c("pop1991", "literacy1991", "scst_share1991",
                  "pre98_water_taps", "pre98_road_km")
balance_form <- reformulate("ReservedSeat", response = balance_vars)
balance_regs <- lapply(balance_form, function(f) feols(f, data))

modelsummary(balance_regs, stars = TRUE)

# 4. Main IV specification -----------------------------------------
iv_formula <- WaterShare ~ FemalePradhan + pop1991 + literacy1991 +
                            scst_share1991 | . -FemalePradhan + ReservedSeat

iv_water <- feols(iv_formula,
                  cluster = ~block, data = data)
summary(iv_water)

# 5. Robustness: add block FE & restrict to West Bengal ------------
iv_blockfe <- feols(update(iv_formula, . ~ . + block | .), 
                    cluster=~block, data = data)
summary(iv_blockfe)

# 6. First-stage F-statistic ---------------------------------------
etable(iv_water, iv_blockfe, fitstat = "ivf")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior from bargaining‐power models and qualitative evidence: women place higher value on drinking water and welfare programs, men on roads and irrigation.

Expected signs:  
•	β(WaterShare) > 0; a female Pradhan raises the water spend share by roughly 6-10 percentage points (≈ 0.3 SD).  
•	β(RoadShare) < 0 by a similar magnitude.  
•	Total expenditure is likely unchanged; it is the composition that shifts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument relevance (F-stat > 10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible ……………………… 0.5  
C3: Independence / random assignment ……………… 1  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ………………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers) ……………………………………… 0.5  

Total = 4 / 5 – generally strong, but exclusion and spillovers merit careful discussion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan leverages the legally mandated, rotating reservation system as an exogenous instrument for female leadership to obtain credible causal estimates of how women in power reshape local public-goods provision.
